#3601. Scott Colom’s Mississippi Votes Are Still Rolling In—and So Are the Views on His Viral Campaign Ads

In an era when short-form-video political messaging reigns supreme, it might be a tiebreaker, and even kingmaker, in Mississippi’s Senate midterm race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom narrowly leads incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as ballots continue to be counted on Thursday, November 5.

On October 13, Colom’s campaign released an ad that opens with a clip from a televised February interview featuring Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer and former agriculture commissioner, responding to a question about rising beef prices by offering that Mississippians “have so many proteins to choose from.” The ad then cuts to a man grilling burgers. “Pick another protein?” he asks. “Sheee-it. I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad appears to have been made by content creator Ryan Sayles. Vanity Fair has reached out to Sayles as well as Colom’s campaign for comment.

The message, which highlighted the Colom campaign’s commitment to cost cutting, capitalized on Hyde-Smith’s gaffe to the tune of more than 2.8 million views between X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook within the first 36 hours, according to the Clarion-Ledger. Former president Barack Obama’s video endorsement emphasizing Colom’s “Christian faith,” released just a day earlier, earned just over 700,000 views on the platforms in nearly double the time.

Colom currently has the edge in the historically deep-red state: If elected, he would become the first Democratic Mississippi Senator in more than 40 years—as part of the blue wave that swept the 2026 midterms, in which Democrats seized back control of both the House and Senate from MAGA-era Republicans. In Mississippi, which President Trump won by roughly 20 points in 2024, Hyde-Smith was favored to win. That is, until mid-October, when one of Colom’s campaign ads went viral, turning the Southern enclave into a surprise battleground state.

The day before Halloween, Colom made waves when he paid tribute to the Oscar-winning Ryan Coogler film Sinners, casting himself and his twin brother, Andrew, as fictional twins Smoke and Stack Moore, both portrayed by Michael B. Jordan in the movie. The film, which was set in the 1932 Mississippi Delta, follows the Black brothers as they try to keep white vampires away from their juke joint. The ad, titled “Sinators,” and released by Colom on October 30 with the disclaimer that “this is a joke!” shows the two men guarding a door as a blonde woman, who seems to be a proxy for Hyde-Smith, tries to enter. Colom says the duo have to “hold her off until the sun rises on Election Day” in the ad, which garnered more than 380,000 views on X alone prior to the November 3 election, as reported by the Sun Herald. If Colom wins, he would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era (1865–1877). VF has reached out to Coogler for comment on Colom’s campaign ad.

Colom’s attention-grabbing content hasn’t come without controversy. During the campaign, the candidate was compelled to delete another ad that featured an artificial-intelligence-generated depiction of Hyde-Smith running away from reporters after the state attorney general Lynn Fitch threatened legal action against him. (Fitch, a Republican, helped support Texas’s lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results, and was also counsel for the petitioner on Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the case which ultimately overturned Roe v. Wade.)

Shortly before the release of the Sinners ad, but after the AI dustup, the Senate Majority PAC, the flagship super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on a broadcast TV and digital ad campaign for Colom. “It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement to The Hill.

Colom, a local prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, seeking her second full term in the Senate, had a past connection heading into this political stand-off. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for federal judge in 2023, citing his support for transgender rights and his having previously been boosted by a George Soros–linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press. Colom told ABC News this “has nothing to do with the run for me…. As a Christian, I forgive her. It’s about the people in Mississippi.”

Since Mississippi elections do not have an automatic recount process, the opponents face a potential legal challenge over the results of their Senate race, in which Colom holds a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith. Colom later echoed a similar sentiment. “It’s not about me. It’s about the people in Mississippi,” the smiling Colom told reporters while speaking to constituents at a local establishment on Thursday morning. “They decided to go in a new direction.”

#3600. Aaron Eckhart's 83-Minute Gritty Neo-Western Becomes A Global Streaming Hit

Thanks to "Yellowstone" and its various offshoots, Paramount+ has become the primary purveyor of neo-Western entertainment in Hollywood. But the streamer isn't just home to wildly popular Taylor Sheridan dramas. It also has a few great neo-Western movies worth a look, and Aaron Eckhart's latest has just topped the streamer's charts worldwide. Unfortunately, "Thieves Highway" isn't available on Paramount+ in the United States. But if you happen to live stateside and have a Hulu subscription, take this as a sign to check out the movie on Hulu/Disney+.

A department of agriculture agent might not seem like the most badass designation for a B-movie hero, but Eckhart is here to surprise you with a film that proves cattle rustling didn't disappear along with the Old West and that livestock agents can hand out some brutal beatdowns. "Thieves Highway" sees Eckhart play a lonely lawman who single-handedly takes on a modern cattle rustling operation and winds up in a fight for his life. It's silly, over-the-top action that's well worth a weekend watch.

"Theives Highway" isn't one of the greatest Westerns of the 2020s, but it deserves more attention than it got upon its initial release. The film stars Aaron Eckhart as widowed Oklahoma livestock agent Frank Bennett, who encounters Devon Sawa's Jones and his gang of livestock thieves while driving home. He decides to try to apprehend them alone, but is quickly overwhelmed and thrust into a fight for his life. Alone and outnumbered, Bennett has to find a way to thwart the cattle rustlers before they can reach the border, while also making it back home in one piece.

The film doesn't have enough reviews on Rotten Tomatoes for a critic score, and its 18% audience score isn't the best advertisement for its quality. Still, Paramount+ viewers seem to be enjoying it. Per streaming viewership tracker FlixPatrol, "Thieves Highway" is sitting at number one on the streamer's movie charts in 18 countries. Even more impressive, the film hit Paramount+ internationally in early November and debuted in the top spot in all 18 of those markets. It's also sitting at number nine in Canada. All of that has made "Thieves Highway" the number one movie on Paramount+ worldwide.

That's not bad for a film nobody had heard of. While "Thieves Highway" is certainly a low-budget actioner of the B-movie variety, Jessie V. Johnson is one of the better directors working in that area, and the film has a compelling premise with its focus on cattle rustling in modern-day Oklahoma. If you're in the United States and intrigued to see what all the fuss is about, the movie is available to stream on Hulu and Disney+ right now.

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is gearing up to make its return on the 2026 TV schedule, and fans should mark their calendars because the release schedule for Season 3 is a bit confusing. The fantasy show isn't doing traditional weekly releases, and it's not going full-binge either; instead, it will be taking a page out of Netflix’s Stranger Things handbook and releasing episodes in blocks. While this does give me a headache, the showrunner's reasoning for it makes perfect sense.

Those with an Amazon Prime subscription will be treated to the first four episodes of Rings of Power Season 3 on November 11. A week later, on November 18, two more episodes will be released. Then, the final two episodes will be released on November 25. In the past, this show has dropped a chunk of episodes at the start and then released one at a time on a weekly basis. However, this model they're using for Season 3 is quite different, and it will give fans the show very fast. It sounds like getting the streaming service to agree to the schedule was a bit of a challenge, as co-showrunner Patrick McKay told io9:

We’re always in conversation with Amazon, and we’re advocating for what we think is best for the show.

It’s not the first time showrunners have had to advocate for a different release strategy with their streaming services. Just last year, the Duffer Brothers sat down with Netflix to persuade them into releasing the final episode of Stranger Things in theaters alongside the streaming service drop. Plus, that final season was released in three chunks between Thanksgiving and the new year. McKay and his co-showrunner J.D. Payne weren’t gunning for a theatrical release, but they did feel strongly about being able to release the show in blocks instead of rolling out episodes weekly, as McKay continued:

We generally, as the creators, feel that the show plays better on a binge because it really is so highly serialized and there are so many storylines. It’s the kind of show, just as viewers, that we find that you really have to pay attention to and you want to get that feeling you get when you’re hooked on a show where it sweeps you away.

As much as I think the binge-watching model is ruining television, I can see why a block release makes sense for Rings of Power. The show is packed with storylines, and they can't all be addressed in every episode, meaning fans would sometimes have to wait weeks before they saw their favorite characters back on screen. That won’t be the case this year, which will be a welcome change, especially after the revelation about what The Stranger’s actual name is.

Season 3 will also feature a time jump, which means there’s going to be even more for fans to catch up on. In an age when everyone’s attention spans are so short, it makes sense that a block schedule would be used so fans don’t forget minor details that might be important in subsequent episodes, which is exactly the point McKay was making, saying:

And we find when you watch it, boom, boom, boom, boom, it sort of works better. So we’re always advocating for more episodes sooner, and then this particular season, we really wanted it to be out by the holidays. We wanted people to be able to binge it over the holidays. So it’ll be a quick release, but then you can watch it at your leisure.

In a way, The Rings of Power release schedule has something for all kinds of television watchers. Fans who want to watch things immediately or prefer a weekly release can engage in mini-binge sessions every seven days. Meanwhile, fans who prefer an hours-long traditional binge session only have to wait three weeks for the entire show to be released instead of six to eight weeks.

It will be interesting to see how the new release schedule affects its viewership, but The Lord of the Rings fandom is huge, and Season 4 is already in development, so I’m sure it will be fine.

If you haven't been watching the show, or need to brush up before Season 3 begins, now is the time to do it!

#3598. Inside Ye’s Yeezy Runway Show in Los Angeles After His Antisemitism Scandals

Once I clawed my way through the crowd of leather pilot jackets and passed the overzealous security guards who checked my ticket thrice, I walked through a borehole into the new Yeezy flagship store in Los Angeles’s Koreatown, where Ye stood off in the corner talking to some professional cool kids. Hundreds of people gathered on Wednesday night inside the white, brightly lit, cavernous space connected by tube-like passages for his label’s first runway show in four years. Rappers Big Sean, Kid Cudi, Rich the Kid, and A$AP Nast showed up—so did influencers Quenlin Blackwell and Fai Khadra. The streamer N3on, Ye’s daughter North, and his wife Bianca Censori also attended. And there were hundreds of unticketed fans waiting outside, hoping to get in.

“I’ve been waiting for a Yeezy show for a minute,” Kid Cudi told a camera crew on his way inside. “It’s just beautiful to see my big bro back out there doing his thing.” The musician’s team said he was “on hiatus” when Vanity Fair reached out for comment afterward. A woman standing next to me online started loudly complaining as people tried to cut her. “I just wanna see Ye,” she moaned.

And there were some other attendees who seemed more interested in making their own content. “I’m trying to network,” N3on told his Kick audience on a livestream from the show. “Everyone’s here bro…I’m looking for some collabs.”

The show started with the sound of the first note (E6) of the piano part at the beginning of Ye’s song Runaway. Models marched around a giant mound in the middle of the room in leather trench coats, militaristic jackets, shorts cut like briefs, and monochrome combat uniforms in shades of bone, charcoal, black, and red. Some of the models wore chunky combat boots that rose up the calf; others balanced on thin stilettos, including a pair of knee-high cream boots that looked like they belonged to a space-age dominatrix. It was utilitarian and a bit fetishy. The pacing of the runway walks was relentless, as if Ye was hitting you over the head with this concept until you thought it was cool. After the show, Ye walked out to a standing ovation, wearing an all-black leather outfit, black military boots, and a huge gold tiger-shaped belt buckle.

There is something fascinating about the fact that Ye can still draw adoring crowds like this one in Koreatown, and sell out football stadiums while other artists find themselves on black lists for doing way less (Javier Bardem, for example, claims he’s lost roles and brand endorsement deals because of his opposition to the war in Gaza). Ye’s last major runway show was in October 2022, during Paris Fashion Week, when he sent models down the runway wearing shirts emblazoned with the words “White Lives Matter.” The stunt led to a public confrontation with then Vogue fashion editor Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, whom Ye proceeded to attack online after she criticized the collection (Vogue, like Vanity Fair, is owned by Condé Nast). The whole thing, plus his breakup with Adidas (a brand that was started by two former members of the Nazi party) over a series of antisemitic comments, amounted to a huge fall from grace for someone who once enjoyed the patronage of Anna Wintour and helped reshape the next generation of streetwear.

One reason for Ye’s continued commercial viability is, of course, his artistic prowess. There are certain artists who become too big to fail, not because they’re too wealthy or too powerful, but because their old work has become so deeply embedded in popular culture that people can’t let it go, while their new work continues to push boundaries. That might be the case for Ye—even if this latest show wasn’t particularly groundbreaking or original. If I’m being generous, the new line was giving Boots, the Netflix military dramedy set in the ’90s about a gay marine. But, given what we know about Ye, parts of the show could’ve also been interpreted as skinhead-coded. And it certainly didn’t feel like I experienced a display of genius—a term we need to stop using to describe Ye. He probably doesn’t need us to put him on that pedestal (his ego is big enough), and I remain skeptical that a truly great artist can be capable of spewing so much hate. Art is about empathy.

I suppose most of the people cheering at Wednesday’s show had learned to compartmentalize. They had found a way to separate the designer who completely changed the sneaker game and ushered in a new era in streetwear from the guy who declared his love for Hitler, threatened to go “DEFCON 3” on Jewish people, and released a song called “Heil Hitler.” Or perhaps they really believed the apology Ye published as an advertisement in The Wall Street Journal earlier this year, in which he attributed his antisemitic behavior in part to bipolar disorder and a brain injury. Or maybe the antisemitism never bothered them in the first place.

I was asked to cover this show because I’m based in LA—I’m typically not a style correspondent. But still, I was plenty curious to see what Ye was up to. On the drive over, I thought about the ethics of covering his first big commercial venture since 2022. Maybe I would be giving him exposure he didn’t deserve. Or, maybe my presence amounted to some kind of tacit endorsement. But I dismissed that thought because I knew plenty of Jews who went to Ye’s concert at NRG Stadium in Houston last week, and I didn’t equate their attendance with bigotry. But it raises a lot of interesting questions about the politics of art and fandom. Does going to see the Michael Jackson movie mean you don’t believe the sexual abuse allegations against him? Do I have to forgive Ye’s antisemitism if I want to keep The College Dropout and My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy in my listening rotation? Maybe it’s kind of similar to how carnivores need to be okay with the murder of animals if they’re going to eat meat. I guess I’d have to be willing to forgive Ye in some sense if I plan to keep singing “couldn’t afford a car, so she called her daughter Alexis,” out loud on the StairMaster at Equinox.

Whatever one thinks of Ye personally, his influence on fashion and music is undeniable. The muted colors, exaggerated proportions and futuristic sneakers that helped define Yeezy have spread through the industry. His fingerprints are all over contemporary fashion, including the celebrity brands that followed in his wake. (Cough cough: Skims and SKYLRK).

Wednesday’s show, titled Season 01, was billed as a reset for Yeezy. So, it makes sense that the show took place in something of a primordial cave. But it’s going to be hard for him to ditch some of the baggage he’s accumulated over the last few years. Standing outside the show was a man wearing a navy suit, white shirt, red tie, and Trump ’28 hat—a loud reminder that Ye hobnobbed with white supremacists like Nick Fuentes and ran for president with the far-right conspiratorial political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos as his campaign manager.

Ye perfectly summed up my feelings about him in one of his own songs. “I miss the old Kanye, straight from the Go Kanye.”

#3597. 10 Hacks Every Google Messages User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Messages is Google's official texting app, and while it hasn't always been first to roll out useful features, it has caught up to what other messaging services offer and has a handful of hidden hacks to make communicating and coordinating with contacts easier and safer. Here are the best tips and tricks that every Google Messages user should know.

Google Messages recently got a Google Keep integration, which allows group chat participants to collaborate on notes and checklists directly in the message thread without having to click over to a separate app. This also centralizes ideas in one place rather than spread across a thread with dozens of separate text messages. Changes to Keep Notes sync automatically for all users. Tap the plus icon in the message compose bar in Google Messages, select Keep Notes, and either choose an existing note or tap to create a new one to be shared in the chat.

Over the last few years, Google has rolled out a number of security features for identifying and defending against scams and fraud spread via calls and text messages. These work by detecting suspected spam and either preventing it from being delivered or hiding it in a separate folder, as well as flagging suspicious links. A newer opt-in enhanced protection mode for Google Messages uses AI to catch more complex threats and alert you if a conversation or unfamiliar link that looks legit might put you at risk. Standard protection is on by default, but you can turn on enhanced protection under Messages settings > Protection & Safety > Spam and scam protection.

If you have an idea you want to write down but not send immediately—because it's outside of work hours or late at night—you can draft it in Google Messages and schedule it for later. "Send later" features in messaging and chat apps are useful for maintaining good boundaries without having to remember to type and send at a different time. Once you've entered your message in the text field, touch and hold Send, choose from the suggested actions, then tap Send again.

Swiping left or right on your conversations in Google Messages will either archive or delete them. You can customize which swipe maps onto which action for quick inbox triaging or disable one or both to prevent accidentally triggering an unwanted action. Tap your profile photo > Message settings > Swipe actions > Customize to select your preferences.

Google Messages has a pinning feature that will anchor conversations at the top of your message history, but you can also star important messages you want to save and return to later. Starring makes it easy to keep track of data like flight information, contacts, or dates that might otherwise get lost in a thread or be difficult to pull up in a basic search—starred messages have their own search filter. Simply tap and hold the message and tap Star at the top, then go to Search conversations > Starred > More options > Starred to see your list of saved messages.

We've all been in the overactive group chat that we don't want to see notifications from in real time but also don't want to leave. You can snooze threads semi-permanently, but you can also turn on a temporary snooze that will lift so notifications restart after a short period of time. This can be useful for threads discussing live events or games you will be catching up on later or if you need silence during a focused work period. Touch and hold the conversation, tap Snooze, then select your duration and tap Snooze to confirm. You can choose from 1 hour, 8 hours, 24 hours, or always.

Google Messages has two group chat modes. Group MMS is your typical group text—it sends a single message to all recipients, and everyone receives replies in the thread. Mass Text, by contrast, is like BCC. This sends your message to each user individually, and replies come only to the original sender. Using this mode allows you to share information with a bunch of people at once without creating the dreaded reply-all thread. You can change your default group messaging settings via profile > Message settings > Advanced > Group messaging.

Google Messages finally launched integrated real-time location sharing earlier this year, which allows you to send your live whereabouts to trusted contacts directly in a message thread. Location sharing makes it easier to coordinate meeting up or let someone know where you are if there are any safety concerns. You can set a limited duration or leave location sharing on indefinitely for specific contacts. Open a conversation and tap Attachment > Real-time location

You don't have to live with the embarrassment of sending a text in error with Google Messages—at least not if you catch the mistake quickly. Google Messages has a "Delete for everyone" function that can remove sent messages from the devices of users who are running the latest version of the app. Conversations must be using RCS for this to work, and you have only a limited window—anywhere from 15 to 40 minutes, according to support documentation—to use the feature before your messages are permanent. Long-press a message to pull up available delete options.

If you want to stay on top of your text threads but get distracted by other things every time you pick up your phone, you can log into the Google Messages web interface on your browser. This also makes it easier to send photos and files from your computer via Google Messages without having to transfer them to your phone first.

#3596. James Gunn Approves Fan-Made Timeline Showing How Clayface And Blue Beetle Fit In The DC Universe

"Clayface" just expanded the DC Universe, giving fans their first introduction to the franchise's live-action Gotham City. The street-level story proved this still-fledgling cinematic enterprise can encompass an R-rated body horror just as easily as a charming crowd-pleaser like 2026's "Superman." Meanwhile, there are plenty of upcoming DCU movies that aim to similarly expand James Gunn and Peter Safran's shared universe. While the DC Studios co-heads are aiming to avoid the complexity of the erstwhile Snyderverse, you'd be forgiven for losing track of the new in-universe timeline. Now, we have an unofficial attempt to make sense of that very thing — and it's just been co-signed by Gunn himself.

User comicbookcollide posted a list of DC Universe projects on Threads in an attempt to arrange the various films and TV series into a coherent in-universe timeline. Turns out, they were pretty much on the money. Gunn responded to the post, writing, "Timelines give me anxiety, but I think this is pretty good." That's about as solid an endorsement for a fan-made timeline as you could hope for — though it should be noted that Gunn stopped short of fully endorsing the post as fact.

This particular timeline of events slots "Clayface" in as the second DCU event/project, listing the events therein as having occurred in 2021. Meanwhile, comicbookcollide also included "Blue Beetle," the 2023 film which belonged to the now-shuttered DC Extended Universe. This particular film, which Gunn has confirmed is canon to the DCU, is listed as having occurred in 2023 just prior to the events of "Creature Commandos" Season 1 — the official first DCU project. That also puts "Blue Beetle" before "Superman" and after the events of "Clayface," "The Suicide Squad," and "Peacemaker" Season 1.

James Gunn was never going to confirm a fan-made DC Universe timeline as 100% accurate and official. But there might be more to his reluctance to fully endorse comicbookcollide's post. While Gunn has said "Blue Beetle" is canon to the DCU, he also made clear there are a few retcons required to make it fit. The same is true of "Peacemaker" Season 1, which originally debuted while the DC Extended Universe was still running. The show received a particularly conspicuous retcon when Gunn and his DC Studios cohorts re-edited the Season 1 finale to include the Justice Gang rather than the former Justice League. Perhaps the fact that "Blue Beetle" isn't fully canon (but still sort-of is) accounts for why Gunn hasn't fully endorsed the fan-made timeline.

The Wrap previously reported that Jaime Reyes/Blue Beetle actor Xolo Maridueña is set to appear in Gunn's "Superman" sequel "Man of Tomorrow," which would fully solidify his original film as having been retconned into the DCU. But there's no doubt Gunn's approach is a little confusing.

Rather than rebooting DC's cinematic universe entirely, the director has tried to keep aspects of the former DCEU while charting a new course. Thus far, that hasn't been too much of an issue, but this is exactly the kind of esoteric minutiae that can turn off mass audiences and lead to widespread so-called superhero fatigue. As such, it is at least reassuring to see all the various DCU projects laid out in a timeline that Gunn has mostly co-signed, even if it all seemed a bit unnecessary from the beginning.

While comicbookcollide's timeline is fairly comprehensive, it does leave out some DCU events. For example, "Lanterns" Episode 1 began by clarifying the DC Universe timeline, revealing that Earth's first Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler), emerged in 1986 and revealed his identity in 1996. This means he had been operating long before the events of "Superman," which took place in 2025. These small but significant developments aren't included in the list posted to Threads, which otherwise does a solid job of making sense of the DCU timeline and combining former DCEU projects (such as the aforementioned "Peacemaker" Season 1, "The Suicide Squad," and "Blue Beetle") into the new chronology.

Meanwhile, Gunn's comment about timelines giving him "anxiety" seems a little baffling. It's his job to stay on top of this stuff and build a shared cinematic universe that maintains a coherent timeline and structure — otherwise DC would just stick with making the so-called "Elseworlds" projects and not worry about the whole interconnected aspect. He also recently appeared on a special "The Suicide Squad: Is It Canon?" podcast, a show specifically designed to clarify how the 2021 movie slots into the DCU and which parts are officially canon. Clearly, Gunn is thinking about these things and has a good idea of how these earlier films mesh with his new vision, to the extent it seems like he enjoys being the only one who really understands it all. Where the anxiety comes from, I'm not sure.

For now, we at least have a better idea of how "Blue Beetle" and "Clayface" fit into the overall plan, and it will be interesting to see how the DCU continues to expand in the coming years.

#3595. How to find Richard the dog in Ocarina of Time

How to identify Richard and complete the quest

Finding Richard is a side quest in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. You might have seen Richard, the adorable dog, during your first visit to Hyrule Castle Town: a white energetic dog that you couldn’t pet because its owner would accuse you of trying to steal her dog. If you visit the town again later, you will learn that Richard has disappeared.

Luckily, you can help the distressed owner to find her precious dog. Below, we explain how to find Richard in the Ocarina of Time remake.

To find Richard, you must visit Hyrule Castle Town during the night and identify it among the running dogs. To know which one is Ricard, you must look for a white dog that will twirl and emit a high-pitched bark when you interact with it. All the other dogs have a deeper bark and briefly stand on their hind legs instead of spinning like Richard does. Since you can only look for Richard at night, consider unlocking the Sun's Song to change the time.

While it is possible to find Richard through trial and error, you don't need to. First look for the white dogs, then interact with them to see how they react. Since there aren't many white dogs, checking each one does not take much time. When I found Richard, he was on the street on the left side of the map, but I can't guarantee that it would always be in the same place for every player.

Once you have interacted with and identified Richard, he will follow you. Head to the street that leads to the entrance of the city to find its owner, then talk to her. After a detailed analysis, she will confirm that that dog is, indeed, Richard, and she will reward you with a Piece of Heart.

If you want to start this quest but Richard hasn't disappeared yet, be sure to deliver Zelda's letter to the guard in Kakariko Village after completing the "Princess of Hyrule Castle" quest. Progressing through the campaign until this point will trigger a change in Hyrule Castle Town and unlock the Richard quest.

While there are obvious frontrunners on the season of Dancing with the Stars airing on the 2026 TV schedule, I’ve always thought Connor Wood could make a deep run on the show. First of all, never underestimate the power of an internet personality. Secondly, and more importantly, he’s so committed to the process and improving so much, it’s easy to see him making it all the way to the end. It turns out I’m not the only one who thinks this, as both Derek Hough and a DWTS champion have predicted that the man who goes by Fibula online will make it all the way to the end.

I feel like it's a big deal when a judge makes a prediction about Dancing with the Stars, so I’m not taking Derek Hough’s words lightly. During an interview with TV Insider, he boldly claimed that he really thinks Connor Wood and his partner Rylee Arnold will be in the finale, stating:

I believe he’ll be in the final. There’s a glow around them. The two of them, I think they’re such a great partnership.

Wood and Arnold really are a wonderful pair, and it’s very clear they adore each other. They are also very funny and endearing, which makes them so gosh darn likable. That could be part of the reason people are voting for him, and why they’ll continue to. Hough made that point clear too, saying:

People love him; I love him. He’s such a good dude; we have the same friends, and he’s a good man. I love him.

Well, there you have it, Derek Hough really thinks Connor Wood will make it to the end, but he's not the only one.

While Derek Hough saying Wood could make the final is huge, there’s another big name who thinks the comedian has what it takes. That person is Joey Graziadei, Season 33’s winner. Speaking to TV Insider about the podcast host, the man who won with Jenna Johnson said:

I will almost guarantee that he makes the finale. I think he can. I think that he’s the perfect blend of his dancing has gotten better, and I would be shocked if he doesn’t have the votes. He seems online to have a really big army behind him and Rylee. He’s just doing it so well.

Joey went on to say that he thinks people can see how committed Wood is to this process, as well as his improvement. In short, “he is what this show is about.” And you know what? Graziadei would know. He won his season of Dancing with the Stars, and he also came in with very little experience. The Bachelor star brought that up too, explaining:

That’s kind of the route I fell under. No one expected me to be good, and I got better throughout, and I think that’s part of the things people look for on that show.

I think Graziadei makes such a good point here, plus he knows from experience. He wasn’t the person on his season with the most dance experience. However, he was so solid all season; he improved big time, and he won. That’s exactly why Connor Wood could make it to the finale too.

The co-host of Brooke and Connor Make a Podcast has shown massive improvement over the weeks, and the joy he and his partner are getting out of this process is infectious. I mean, I wanted to scream with excitement just like they did when they got their first tens (and an eight from Shirley Ballas, which is high praise from her considering how low she scored other contestants) on Halloween Night.

Also, you can’t look past the passionate fans Wood and Arnold have. He has 1.4 million followers on TikTok, and she has 2.1 million. Their videos consistently get millions and millions of views, and we cannot forget the ultra-viral situation that was launched by him saying he had a crush on Jennifer Lawrence and her replying that she saw him on 8th Avenue drinking a smoothie and he paid her no mind.

All I’m saying here is it’s obvious people ride for Papa (which is a nickname Wood has had to try and explain many times), and that mixed with his commitment and improvement on the show is a recipe made for a finalist.

Now, to see if he can go the distance, you can watch Dancing with the Stars every Tuesday at 8 p.m. ET on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription.

#3593. 10 Shows Like 'VisionQuest' You Should Watch Next

Following the events of WandaVision (and, slightly more tangentially, Agatha All Along), VisionQuest returns to the story of Marvel's favorite synthic being, an artificial creation who fights supervillains and ponders the nature of his own existence, rather than more typical AI pursuits like creating deep fakes.

White Vision (the character, not the political agenda) is a copy of the Vision who died two Avengers movies ago. He's living within his own mind on a fantasy country estate while on the run from bounty hunters and in pursuit of his semi-fictional son. In that spirit, here are 10 more science fiction shows that involve artificial people and/or elaborate constructed realities.

In the near-future world, highly advanced “synths” are commonplace, doing the work that regular humans can’t be bothered with. These beings are treated as entirely disposable sources of cheap labor, despite their apparent burgeoning humanity. The first season introduces the Hawkins family, who buy (on sale) a domestic servant synth named Anita (Gemma Chan); mom Laura is a little uncomfortable with the arrangement, especially when she finds her husband having sex with Anita, who has her own complicated backstory. Humans interrogates the ways humans always seem to find excuses to dehumanize others, which is just the type of thing that sci-fi is pretty great at. Stream Humans on Peacock, Prime Video, and Tubi.

One of the smartest recent shows is a dark comedy based on the Hugo-Award winning book series by Martha Wells. Alexander Skarsgård is the title's hilariously deadpan robot, a private "security construct" who's managed to hack its way through its own programming and gain free will—which it mostly wants to use to binge its favorite streaming shows. It can't just run off for fear of drawing attention, but the self-named Murderbot (it's being ironic, kinda) is content to do the bare minimum when it's assigned to a team of naive hippie researchers who don't see the need for a killer security robot—at least, not until they're enmeshed in a complicated capitalist plot in which they're all just cogs. Stream Murderbot on Apple TV.

From playwright Tearrance Arvelle Chisholm (Hooded: Or Being Black for Dummies), this show stars Okieriete Onaodowan as the title character, an inhabitant of an alternate present who is turning 33 and pursuing therapy for the first time. He's offered the chance to use DIRT (Digital Immersive Reality Therapy), in which he can visit and view other versions of himself, as long as he doesn't interfere. Which, of course, he does, with results that are sometimes poignant and sometimes funny. Hard to believe that this clever show almost wound up in the bin, a victim of that stupid moment a couple of years ago when streamers and studios were shelving otherwise great projects for tax reasons. No robots here, but a human exploring a complex world inside his own head. Stream Demascus on Tubi.

In this more darkly dangerous vision of a virtual world, video-game-obsessed Arisu gets his wish, after a fashion; he finds himself, along with a couple of friends, transported to an alternate, eerily abandoned version of Tokyo—the title’s Borderland—vividly brought to life via clever green screen work. The three are directed to an arena and given the instructions for the game, which they’ll be playing whether they want to or not. The first competition involves a locked-room-style puzzle; if they fail, the room goes up in flames with them in it—think Ready Player One, with deadlier stakes. There are games each night, though the rules allow for winners to get time off. There are a lot of rules, actually, but the games are cleverly and sadistically constructed. Stream Alice in Borderland on Netflix.

Though ostensibly an X-Men spinoff, this phantasmagoric show from Noah Hawley (Fargo, Alien: Earth) stands entirely on its own, taking place largely inside the headspace of a deeply troubled man. Dan Stevens plays David Haller, diagnosed with schizophrenia and possessed of tremendous psychic abilities. In one of the many psychiatric hospitals to which he's been committed, he meets first the free-wheeling Lenny (Aubrey Plaza) and then Syd (Rachel Keller), who can trade bodies with anyone she touches. Veering in and out of trippy astral planes and deeply damaged psyches, David soon comes to realize that he's not crazy—and also that he's probably not the hero of the story, even as he's caught between the authorities who'd like to use him for his power and the Shadow King who's been haunting his mind since childhood. Stream Legion on Hulu.

Just a science fiction action comedy about a nun married to literal Jesus on a quest to save the world from the title's artificial intelligence by finding the Holy Grail alongside her ex-boyfriend. So, yeah, there’s a lot going on in Mrs. Davis—sometimes a little too much, but the show gets major points for ambition. Betty Gilpin holds everything together as Sister Simone, playing it straight in an extremely over-the-top world. It’s refreshing to see a show that’s so unafraid to take big swings, and it works much more often than it should. Though it was cancelled after one season, it ends reasonably well, and, like co-creator Damon Lindelof’s HBO series Watchmen, would probably be best served by remaining a one-and-done. Stream Mrs. Davis on Peacock.

A charming comedy-drama set in a science fiction world, Robbie Amell stars as Nathan Brown, a young computer programmer who's also recently deceased. In the future of 2033, humans have the option of having their consciousnesses uploaded into virtual worlds post-mortem and Nathan's is chosen for him by his rich and rather possessive girlfriend. The exclusive afterlife setting of Lakeview is stifling, as is the fact that said girlfriend has a say in his perpetual existence. He's on the brink of despair until he strikes up a friendship with Nora (Andy Allo), his very-much-alive customer service rep. Stream Upload on Prime Video and Hulu.

Tricky to recommend, given that the show's four seasons saw a period of decline followed by a cancellation just when it was getting really good again—however, when Westworld was cooking (as in its addictive first season), there was nothing else like it on television. Set, initially, in a high-tech, near-future amusement park designed to appeal to wealthy clientele, the show finds the lifelike androids created to service the guests gradually waking up to their disposability. In the best tradition of sci-fi, this one's less about AI than it is about a world of disposable beings existing purely at the whim, and for the amusement of, the ultra-wealthy. Which is definitely not a 100% relatable metaphor. Buy Westworld from Prime Video.

You've likely seen this one if you're watching VisionQuest, but it's worth mentioning as not only a fairly essential preface, but also one of the best (and most distinctive) bits of Marvel media...ever? (Agatha All Along is also great, but less essential to Vision's narrative). At least initially, WandaVision confused dedicated Marvel fans as much as noobs, making it a unique on-ramp, even if it does have many threads connected to the broader superhero universe. Its story of a grieving witch living out her sitcom fantasies is an impressive swing into the surreal, well worth it if you’re content to go along for a weird and surprisingly emotional ride. Stream WandaVision on Disney+.

#3592. 5 Years Ago Today: Marvel Released One Of The Most Polarizing Superhero Movies In History

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

For more than a decade, the Marvel Cinematic Universe was as bulletproof as it gets in Hollywood. Even "Thor: The Dark World" became a box office hit while also setting a low bar for the MCU from a critical perspective. But things changed in the 2020s, and that truly became evident five years ago when Marvel Studios released one of the most divisive superhero movies in recent memory, if not ever.

Directed by Chloé Zhao, who was hot off of the Best Picture-winning "Nomadland," "Eternals" was supposed to be the start of something new within the MCU. Not unlike how "Guardians of the Galaxy" opened up the cosmic side of the universe, these characters were meant to be a major part of the Multiverse Saga. Instead, it was a one-and-done experiment that, five years removed, continues to divide fans.

The early buzz for "Eternals" called it a sprawling superhero movie unlike any other or a complicated mess, depending on who you asked. Not much has changed. Some people have come around to it, others still strongly dislike it. What remains true is that the divisive nature of this sweeping superhero epic proved that the bulletproof nature of the MCU had its limits, and clearly changed plans that Marvel Studios had in place.

The movie focuses on a team of ancient aliens that's been living on Earth in secret for thousands of years. An unexpected tragedy forces them out of the shadows and they are forced to reunite against mankind's most ancient enemy, the Deviants. It boasts a stellar cast led by Gemma Chan (Sersi), Richard Madden (Ikaris), Angelina Jolie (Thena), Salma Hayek (Ajak), and Kumail Nanjiani (Kingo).

Kumail Nanjiani, in particular, went through an impressive physical transformation for the role. Naniani has conflicted feelings about changing his body to play a superhero, but he clearly thought this was going to be a role he would revisit many times. That didn't pan out.

"Eternals" was Marvel Studios' first movie to get a "rotten" score on Rotten Tomatoes, meaning that less than 60% of the approved critics who reviewed it gave it a positive review. As of this writing, it holds a 48% approval rating on the site. That mixed response led to the movie fighting an uphill battle at the box office at a time when theaters were still trying to get back on their feet during the Covid-19 pandemic. For the first time in a long time, word of mouth wasn't on Marvel's side.

The movie made just $402 million at the global box office, which would be solid for many blockbusters but is a sad sum by MCU standards, especially on a reported $200 million budget. By contrast, "Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings" made $432 million, but that was on a smaller $150 million budget and against solid reviews. All the same, "Shang-Chi 2" still hasn't happened.

Marvel's plans to further explore the Eternals on screen were scrapped in light of the film's reception. Plot threads that were introduced never paid off, such as seeing Kit Harington's Dane Whitman become the Black Knight or teasing the arrival of Mahershala Ali's Blade, which will now never happen. (Marvel also seemingly forgot about that large Celestial that was emerging from the ocean, which was completely ignored until last year's "Captain America: Brave New World.")

The "Eternals" credits scenes also meant big things for the future of the MCU, including introducing Harry Styles as Starfox. Five years later, it's almost like that never happened.

What the heck went wrong? Going back to /Film's original review, it dubbed "Eternals" as a wildly ambitious but tonally uneven epic. This movie tried to introduce nearly a dozen major characters and a history that spans centuries, while also including a major love story, gigantic god-like beings in space, and deliver villains that felt worthy of all this chaos. There were a lot of plates to spin, and it's easy to imagine Chloé Zhao's vision clashing with Marvel Studios' desires.

This is right up there with legendarily divisive superhero movies from the past. That includes Zack Snyder's "Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice," which I hated at the time but feel conflicted about now. Snyder is probably the king of divisive comic book cinema, but for a long time, Marvel was seen as the king of the hill that could do no wrong. This was the first instance of the MCU doing something that was viewed by many as "wrong."

I personally count "Eternals" as one of my favorite superhero movies of the 2020s, and I'm not alone. "Finally got around to 'Eternals' on my watch through of everything, it was really good?? I'm so annoyed they scrapped the sequel," Threads user curtain_callme said in September of this year. "Unpopular opinion but I actually really enjoyed The Eternals," said Brittany Kerperian on Threads in October.

It seems for every hater this movie has, there's someone who loves it. That's the very definition of divisive. It's not something the MCU had been accustomed to being in 2021, but it's certainly a reputation the film still has to reckon with.

You can grab "Eternals" on 4K, Blu-ray or DVD from Amazon.

The holiday season has officially begun, and while there are dozens of upcoming Christmas movies to watch, it’s always nice to revisit some of the best Christmas movies ever made, like Elf. Despite the Will Ferrell flick being over 20 years old, there are still so many stories coming out that have never been told before. Now, even more stories are coming out thanks to a new behind-the-scenes book co-written by Elf costar Andy Richter, titled Elf Unwrapped: Behind the Scenes of a Modern Christmas Classic.

Back in 2020, the classic Christmas film was featured on an episode of the Netflix docuseries The Christmas Movies That Made Us. Fans learned a lot of behind-the-scenes facts about the Jon Favreau-directed flick, including the dark ending the film almost received. Elf super fans already know that a large chunk of the interior scenes of the film were shot at an abandoned mental institution. Part of this was to keep costs down since the film was made on a $33 million budget. Richter talked about it with Us Weekly:

There was this old mental hospital that had a couple of empty wings, and that’s where the offices are, the Hobbs’ home, the mailroom; almost all the interiors of the movie are in a mental hospital that was still functioning a little bit. There was still a wing of the hospital that had patients in it.

Money wasn’t the only reason for the unusual filming location, according Ritcher told the outlet. The studio and soundstage space was limited due to a“big vampire movie” that was filming at the same time, so the production design team behind Elf made the unusual filming location work. It turned the space into the Gimbels department store, Greenway Press, and the Hobbs’ apartment. As magical as the locations looked on screen, some actors still found filming at the semi-functioning mental hospital unsettling, including Richter, as he said in the interview:

I wasn’t wandering around.. I went to the set. I went to the trailer. I got in the van. I went back to the hotel.

While filming aimed to stay on the abandoned side of the hospital, portions of the location were still occupied by patients. It’s unclear if any patients actually saw Ferrell traipsing around in his iconic green costume inspired by Rankin/Bass’s elves in Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer, but Ritcher did speculate about what they might have thought if they caught a glimpse of the SNL alum:

Will was all over that place for a month or two, like what people were thinking? Patients were looking out the window and seeing this guy in February wandering around in an elf costume, and maybe recognizing, ‘Hey, isn’t that Will Ferrell?’

Ferrell himself had some apprehensions about the costume the first time he tried it on, so it’s valid for Richter to consider what outsiders who had no idea a Christmas movie was being filmed next door might have thought. Thankfully, it all worked out, and Elf continues to be a holiday movie must-watch for families.

Elf Unwrapped: Behind the Scenes of a Modern Christmas Classic is available at bookstores now, but if you want a more instant Elf fix, you can stream the film with an HBO Max subscription. And who knows, maybe Ferrell will dress up as Buddy the Elf once again to help promote the book.

#3590. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3589. AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

When we first wrote about the coming release of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the first fully AI-generated feature film being self-distributed into movie theaters in the U.S., it would’ve been easy to write the whole thing off as a stunt.

Coming from YouTuber Gossip Goblin, who has an impressive and loyal following, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” started earning comps from the press (and from the producers themselves) to the success Markiplier found when he self-released his film “Iron Lung” and made $50 million worldwide in the process. Would that success translate for an AI movie? A recent example from China suggests that may not be the case. Related Stories Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’ Sony Pictures Classics Buys Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s ‘Violette’

It’s clear though the team behind “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is treating this like a real project that needs to be seen in theaters and is worthy of serious critical consideration, and they’re doing that with real marketing dollars behind its theatrical push.

Today, Gossip Goblin announced that pop star Grimes is set to make a cameo in his film “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” as is YouTuber Mike Majlak, and their involvement is being revealed via a massive Times Square ad campaign that is also launching today, all ahead of the film’s release next month on December 4. Gossip Goblin is even launching a contest for people to use AI to create their own short films within the universe of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” that can net the winning creator $15,000.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” also sparked some headlines in the last few months with the news that the producers are plotting an Oscar campaign for Best Animated Feature. Turns out some FYC screenings have already started and a digital campaign begins at the end of November. All of the above suggests some real belief in the project, and with a collective 16 million views of the trailer thus far, they have reason to believe.

“We’ve been heartened already by the reaction,” producer Edward Saatchi of Fable Studios said in a statement. “One Oscar-Nominated animated film director compared ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ after seeing it to ‘2001,’ and we’ve had great feedback from Pixar folks (part of Fable’s team is ex-Pixar and we hugely respect their work).”

Zack London, the man behind the moniker Gossip Goblin, in speaking with IndieWire ahead of the announcement, said he’s “fully cognizant” of the controversy around putting a movie made with AI into theaters, and he acknowledges that all of this is “a big, unproven hypothesis.” But he says it would be “disingenuous to write it all off” as just an AI movie or not a real project.

Getting screens is easy, but the real battle is making people believe there are actually humans behind this movie, even if the images are all generated by AI. Roughly 30 to 35 people are credited in the making of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” and a behind-the-scenes documentary that is also in the works is aimed to humanize the process of making the movie. It includes interviews with the film’s composer and voice actors and shows its Foley guy doing real post-production work. Even the act of getting a real person like Grimes in the film — whose image is generated to resemble her but who does real voice acting — required an elaborate process of photo mashing atop existing character design to fit her into the movie, as well as contacting the model makers themselves to remove built-in censors for generating images of a public figure’s likeness.

On one hand, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” can be viewed as a scrappy indie made by a team of creatives, not just a sole prompter working alone, making a movie that wouldn’t exist otherwise. On the other hand, many would argue that the visuals on display would normally require a team of thousands to bring to life along with millions of dollars. Depending on where you fall on that spectrum may determine whether you also buy a ticket to see it.

But London and Saatchi have grander ambitions with “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” and AI filmmaking beyond just what it can do at the box office. Saatchi says that for as many great CG animated films have been released in the last 30 years since “Toy Story” first hit theaters, they’ve arguably all looked similar and been made with the same techniques. He views “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” as the next “Toy Story” moment in animation, with a movie that aims to look psychedelic and otherworldly, something that looks unique and looks like it could only be the product of AI generative models. Other films may use AI to create something cheaply that looks like a Pixar movie, but London wanted to make something that looked like nothing else.

“Pixar set the look for animated films in the ’90s — they didn’t use technology to more cheaply make a film that looked like ‘Beauty and the Beast,’ they created a radically new aesthetic with ‘Toy Story,'” Saatchi said. “That’s what ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ represents: a wild new aesthetic for animated films that will define much of animated, actor-voiced films in the coming decades. This is that ‘Toy Story’ moment for our generation — a radical departure for animated films — you only need to see Grimes’ brilliant performance in the film to understand how much things are about to change for animated movies. And we hope the Academy will recognize that a film that is seminal (the first AI film), wildly technically novel and most importantly good deserves a nomination.”

#3588. All Great Fairy's Fountain locations in Ocarina of Time

Great Fairy's Fountains are home to, well, Great Fairies in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. The Great Fairies are your gateway to magic and abilities. They'll give you spells that let you create fire, teleport in and out of dungeons, and grant yourself temporary invulnerability.

However, the Great Fairies are hidden away across Hyrule, and they're pretty hard to find. That's not all though, as in the remake, you have to offer the fairies rupees before they'll provide you with any gifts.

Here's where to find every Great Fairy Fountain in the Ocarina of Time remake, as well as what abilities you'll receive and how many rupees you have to offer to each Great Fairy.

There are six Great Fairy's Fountains in Ocarina of Time, and each Great Fairy will provide you with a unique reward if you can provide them with enough rupees.

The Great Fairies can be found in the following locations:

For their exact locations, check out the sections below.

The first Great Fairy's Fountain can be found at the top of Death Mountain Trail, but you'll first need to unlock the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you have the Bomb Bag, take the path that takes you toward Death Mountain Crater, which is the easternmost path on Death Mountain Trail. Blow up the rocks blocking your way up, and make your way to the stone arch at the top. Go to the end of the tunnel, and the volcano will erupt, launching molten rocks onto the path in front of you. Avoid the rocks and run up the hill as fast as you can. Take out the three Skullwalltulas on the wall, and climb to the top.

On your left, you'll find Kaepora Gaebora and a breakable rock wall behind him. Blow up the wall and play Zelda's Lullaby on the Triforce inside. The Great Fairy will speak to you, and tell you that she'll grant you a new power if you put 25 rupees into the fountain.

Pay her 25 rupees, and you'll unlock magic power and Din's Fire. Magic power is a resource used to cast spells, like Din's Fire. Din's Fire costs two magic power, and when you cast it, fire will spread outwards, dealing fire damage to anything nearby.

The second Great Fairy's Fountain is located on the way to Hyrule Castle, but it's only reachable by young Link. Additionally, like the previous Great Fairy's Fountain, you need the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you climb up the vines and go past the first gate, you'll see a rock wall on the right side of the path. Break it with a bomb and you'll find a tunnel that leads to the Great Fairy.

This time, you need to offer her 50 rupees, but she'll give you Gift of Improved Spin. Now, you can hold down the attack button to charge up a spin attack with magic power. The attack itself won't cost any magic power, but it'll deal additional damage.

The third Great Fairy's Fountain is located at the Zora Fountain. To enter, you'll need the Bomb Bag from Dodongo Cavern.

After you get King Zora to move, head behind him and you'll enter Zora Fountain. Go to the southeast corner of the map, and blow up the rock wall in the corner. Enter the cave, and you'll find the next Great Fairy.

Offer the Great Fairy 100 rupees, and you'll learn Farore's Wind, a spell that allows you to create a warp point in a dungeon for two magic power.

The fourth Great Fairy's Fountain is found in Death Mountain Crater, but first, you need to complete the Fire Temple and unlock the Megaton Hammer. Lastly, make sure you're in the future, and you have the Goron Tunic equipped.

From the Fire Temple warp point, head across the bridge to the east and cross the gap. Follow the path to the south, and you'll see a black rock embedded in the wall. Break it with the Megaton Hammer, and you'll discover the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Give her 200 rupees, and she'll give you the Gift of Doubled Magic, which will double your magic power bar.

The fifth Great Fairy's Fountain is located in Evil Desert Colossus, which is essentially the entrance to the Spirit Temple. You'll reach this area after traveling through the Mirage Desert.

Break the rock wall on the north side of the zone, and you'll find the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Put 300 rupees into the fountain, and you'll receive Nayru's Love, which will make you temporarily invulnerable for four magic power.

The sixth and final Great Fairy's Fountain is just outside of Ganondorf's Castle, but first, you need the Golden Gauntlets from the Shadow room inside the castle.

Before you cross the bridge into Ganondorf's Castle, you'll find a huge black and gold rock to the east. Pick it up and throw it away to find the entrance to the Great Fairy's Fountain.

Offer the Great Fairy 500 rupees, and you'll receive the Gift of Halved Damage. This will literally halve the amount of damage you receive from any damage source.

#3587. Project Hail Mary's Andy Weir Has Tried To Write Screenplays, But Feels 'Constrained' By This Obstacle [Exclusive]

"Project Hail Mary" was based on Andy Weir's 2021 novel of the same name, and by this point it seems as though the author has a knack for stories that play well on the big screen. "Project Hail Mary" dominated the box office upon its March 2026 release, and the 2015 adaptation of his book "The Martian" saw similar commercial success. Both were also met with critical acclaim. As such, it wouldn't seem all that silly for Weir to consider going straight to the screenplay with his future projects and skipping the novel stage altogether. But it seems the writer feels constrained by the idea of working in a visual medium.

/Film's Jeremy Mathai spoke with Weir, who referenced an audiobook called "Exoplanet" that he executive produced. This particular audiobook is an Audible Original sci-fi thriller that plays more like a movie than a book, using sound effects to convey action rather than a narrator providing a play-by-play of events. This, it seems, was a challenge for Weir, who likened it to his difficulties with writing screenplays.

"If you're writing a book, which is what I do, I can just throw in a paragraph of exposition and explain things directly to the reader and that's done," he explained. "You can't do that in an audiobook unless you have a narrator." According to Weir, "Exoplanet" writer Benjamin Percy immediately shut down the idea of having a narrator for the audiobook. "Everything is sounds that are happening in the setting," continued Weir. "I'm like, 'Okay, that makes it harder. It's your funeral.' But [Percy] pulled it off. He did a great job." Interestingly, it's this same challenge that has held Weir back from writing a movie script, despite his efforts to give it a try.

Andy Weir is currently working on his next book which looks set to tackle a hot button topic by focusing on artificial intelligence. Meanwhile, many fans are surely hoping for a sequel to "Project Hail Mary." But it seems the author isn't quite ready for that yet — thought that could very well change in the near future. What he almost certainly won't be doing, however, is writing a screenplay.

As Weir told /Film, "I've tried my hand at writing scripts and screenplays in the past, and I've always felt really constrained and claustrophobic by that because you have very little space to do things." The "That" to which Weir refers is the lack of being able to insert a paragraph of exposition to explain things to readers as straightforwardly as possible. Weir continued:

"Exposition now has to be done through dialogue or visuals. Usually visuals. Visuals do a great job of exposition because you can see the whole everything that's going on, and you don't need to describe actions, you can show them. But in an audiobook, you can't have paragraphs of the exposition and you can't have visuals showing you everything that's going on. So it's very constrained."

Based on his comments about visuals being a great way to convey exposition, It sounds as though Weir would at least be more open to writing a film than a narrative audiobook along the lines of "Exoplanet." For now, however, it seems as though he's happy sticking to novels, which is no doubt fine with both his fans and studios, who, as evidenced by "Project Hail Mary" becoming one of the best movies of 2026, will continue to benefit from great films based on his ideas regardless.

#3586. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.
