What happened to Disney theme parks being the happiest place on Earth?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Disney theme parks are supposed to be the happiest place on earth, where you spend time making memories with family and loved ones. That is, until someone gets into an all-out brawl in the line for Avatar Flight of Passage in Pandora – The World of Avatar inside Disney’s Animal Kingdom, and it results in a lawsuit. Apparently, the individuals involved had been arguing for the entirety of their 80-minute wait, and it finally reached a boiling point, leading to several people seemingly getting physical.

While I find it wild that this happened at all, what makes it even wilder is the fact that this is not the first time a brawl has taken place in a ride queue. Line cutting at Indiana Jones Adventure at Disneyland led to an incident when the person who was doing the cutting hit a man who said something about it, which incited a brawl and resulted in the attacked man sustaining a minor injury.

Pertaining to the fight in Pandora, a series of Reddit posts point to an unknown cause for the arguing between two groups, stating that it didn’t appear to have anything to do with cutting in line. Honestly, regardless of what sparked the fighting, that kind of behavior can’t and shouldn’t be tolerated, and apparently Morgan & Morgan feels the same way, as they’re suing Disney on behalf of a family that was struck several times.

In a statement to Florida Politics, Morgan & Morgan's founder John Morgan and attorney Christopher Ryan explained what reportedly happened to their clients. They also stated the family's expectation for a safe trip at Disney World:

Our clients were on a family vacation at Disney’s Animal Kingdom when they were confronted by a group of adults in line for Avatar Flight of Passage. The encounter allegedly escalated into a physical altercation in which our clients, including their teenage daughter, were struck several times. Families come to Disney expecting to be safe.

In the complaint, it's explained that this group "allegedly pushed Plaintiff and her family, climbed over queue barriers, and struck Plaintiff." It also states that the plaintiff sustained "bodily injuries and damages."

The lawsuit also accused employees of not monitoring the queue, failing to perform adequate crowd control, and not properly de-escalating the situation.

Millions of people visit Disney theme parks every year, and even though these stories of bad behavior tend to make headlines, it does involve a relatively very small number of individuals in comparison. That’s not to say any instance of violence is acceptable (it’s very much not okay). Whether it’s two families throwing fists at Magic Kingdom or a fistfight in Mickey’s Toontown at Disneyland, or even that scuffle over a Disney World photo op, this should just not be happening in any capacity.

In the past, viral videos of Disney World skirmishes tend to get a lot of attention. Lifetime bans from Disney Parks can be lifted, but it requires those banned to send letters of apology to request that the ban be lifted, and it’s very rare that the decision gets reversed.

Sometimes, lawsuits happen too, which is what it has come to after the brawl that broke out on Flight of Passage.

#3584. Why Godzilla Minus Zero Is Rated R

This article contains light spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

For about as long as the Motion Picture Association (formerly "of America") has existed, the conventional wisdom has been that blockbuster genre movies should receive the most inviting rating possible. This concept has existed at least since Steven Spielberg's "Jaws" took the movie industry and pop culture by storm, as its PG rating allowed a wide audience to experience it. Certainly there have been exceptions, most famously at the hands of Spielberg himself, whose 1984 output revealed the necessity for a rating in between PG and R: the PG-13.

This middle ground rating then became the go-to standard for films that are edgy and adult without crossing a line into becoming too much for young teens. Its popularity has resulted in many filmmakers pushing its limits, especially as it came to be known as essentially the default movie rating. So far, every "Godzilla" film has received a rating of PG-13 or lower, as most of the movies involve giant monster-on-giant monster violence (thus meaning it's impossible to emulate in real life, as per the MPA's general view on violence).

However, that has now changed with the release of "Godzilla Minus Zero," which has been given an R rating by the MPA. At first blush, it might seem that this is the "Godzilla" franchise's move to appeal to an edgier audience, in the same way the Marvel Cinematic Universe was only too happy to make "Deadpool and Wolverine" a hard-R. Yet "Minus Zero" isn't R-rated merely for surface-level indulgences like harsh language, extreme violence, or even sex. Instead, "Godzilla Minus Zero" earns the R for two very specific reasons, both of which make the higher rating more understandable.

Ever since the very first "Godzilla" in 1954, the giant monster has been intentionally positioned as an allegory for the ravages of war — specifically, war with atomic weapons, whose devastation Japan had recently experienced. Though Ishirõ Honda's film is a much more thoughtful and somber affair than modern audiences would expect, it's still got enough B-movie flavor to explain why the franchise went on to become increasingly focused on spectacle and even more kid-friendly. While the darkness inherent in "Godzilla" has cropped up in several movies since, the allegorical nature of the character is usually kept to subtext.

Writer/director Takashi Yamazaki takes the franchise further in "Godzilla Minus Zero" by depicting real-life war violence: the immediate aftermath of the US bombing of Hiroshima. In the film, the fictional character Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka) is one of the few survivors of the attack, and we're shown a flashback in which he finds the charred remains of his family.

The upsetting reality of this moment not only fuels the themes of the film, but directly informs Murakami's character, as we learn that his plan is to lure Godzilla to New York City and have the beast attack America. In this brief but powerful fantasy sequence, we see Godzilla shoot his heat rays at the city, causing people's faces to melt off before they incinerate. It's a sequence which does something rare, especially for blockbuster genre films: it depicts an intentional act of genocide on Americans. It's a moment reminiscent of something like "Terminator 2" (which Yamazaki was inspired by), yet even more pointed given the emotion behind it. As such, it makes sense that the MPA would consider it rougher material than previous "Godzilla" movies.

As many have pointed out during the MPA's 60-odd year existence, the organization's rationale for a film's rating is often frustratingly vague. Many filmmakers are annoyed by the process of submitting and resubmitting their movie to get their desired rating, with many decisions coming down to the tiniest omission of a handful of frames, as opposed to large swathes of material. While the MPA's rulings are made on a literal case-by-case basis, the general idea seems to be that they're usually judging a film by its overall tone and effect on an audience, rather than ticking checkboxes. While some elements like nudity and more than one F-bomb in the dialogue are near-guaranteed criteria for an R, some movies earn the rating through what the MPA likes to call "thematic elements."

As such, the R rating for "Godzilla Minus Zero" is more of a cumulative one than anything else. Even if the Hiroshima flashback and NYC dream sequence were edited out, the film might edge close to an R solely for its grisly fight sequences between Godzilla and King Ghidorah. Both kaiju are particularly vicious in the way they take advantage of their respective regenerative powers, with the monsters ripping off each other's heads and limbs, and we see sinewy tendons stretching before they snap. Although it's still fantasy monster violence, when the film as a whole is taken into account, it does feel like giving it a PG-13 would be inappropriate, too. Ultimately, the rating is a reflection of how strong Takashi Yamazaki's filmmaking is. It makes "Godzilla Minus Zero" the latest in a proud lineage of light R-rated films, meaning it's likely to become a gateway genre movie for generations to come.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

The American Cinematheque Awards Gala is officially back on with actor Robert Pattinson, star of several films from 2026, from “Primetime” and “The Drama,” to “The Odyssey” and “Dune: Part Three,” as the 40th recipient. Riley Green is at the top of his game, with seven number one country songs, a spot as a coach on the long-running singing competition The Voice, currently in Season 30 on the 2026 TV schedule, and a well-received guest run on the Yellowstone spin-off Marshals. And while he might have recently made People Magazine’s Sexiest Man Alive issue, understandably so with his down-home appeal, he’s not looking to use that title to get himself out of bachelorhood anytime soon.

Whether he’s on tour as he takes his country crooning around the world or he’s in Los Angeles coaching a team of singers hoping to someday achieve the status of The Voice’s superstar coaches, Riley Green is booked and busy, and more concerned about finding time to spend with family than a girlfriend. While chatting with People about being selected for the sexiest list, he said he’s open to love but admitted to not even seeing his own dog in a month, so now is just probably not the best time. I haven’t seen Carl, my dog, in a month. I struggle to think there’s a girl that, you know… I can barely make this lifestyle work. It seems like the 38 year-old who likes to smack talk his fellow coaches on The Voice (especially O.G. American Idol winner Kelly Clarkson), has given the idea of love some definite thought. He’s very clear about the demands of his career and is riding that wave because he knows that his schedule likely won’t always be this hectic and the current high might not always be at the same level it is now.

For now, the “Worst Way” singer who even has his own customized Big Red Chair on The Voice is focusing on family. When you’re on the road 200-plus days a year, and also spending time in Los Angeles with coaching duties, hoping a member from Team Riley will take it all in Season 30, working in a FaceTime with your adorable nephew is about all the time you can spare. Green explained:

My lifestyle has just got to change a little bit. And I think that what gets me by now, without having those things that I’m kind of hoping for is, I get to FaceTime my nephew Joe, you know, and see what he’s doing and watch him play sports and catching up with my family. We’re all still really close, so they make it bearable in a pretty hectic lifestyle right now.

Constantly being on the road while touring can make any singer feel adrift, no matter how successful they are, so it’s great that Riley Green has close family that he can feel anchored by. Sure, the multi-talented performer who has added acting to his list of skills steals hearts and wins over the love of his growing fan base. But it’s probably a good thing that he wants to wait until he has the time to devote to focusing on just one woman before jumping into a relationship that he can’t fully be a part of. #3579. ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

Among the bleakest films ever made, Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” (1977) famously ends not with the suicide of its title character, but with a haunting coda in which a chicken pecks at a miniature piano inside a surreal roadside tourist trap’s coin-operated display. It’s a visual metaphor for the inescapable banality of life on Earth, and for the dehumanizing work people are forced to do to disguise the many failures of the American Dream. It’s also the last thing that Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis saw before he killed himself. “Look into the eyes of a chicken,” Herzog has said, “and you will see real stupidity. It is a kind of bottomless stupidity, a fiending stupidity. They are the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world.” Related Stories Robert Pattinson to Receive 2026 American Cinematheque Award AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

That sentiment has long endured as modern cinema’s definitive stance on chickens (despite Aardman’s best efforts), but now, after witnessing the 50 years of entropy that followed “Stroszek,” Hungarian filmmaker György Pálfi is crying fowl. Chickens are not the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world, he contends. We are. How can you tell? Easy: Just look at us through the eyes of a chicken.

A cute, cockeyed yarn that unspools like a feathered cross between “EO” and “Flow,” Pálfi’s “Hen” tells the story of a jet-black Leghorn chicken who escapes a Greek factory farm after she’s plucked from the rest of her flock because of the color of her plumage. A worker decides to take the bird home so that his wife can serve it for dinner, but our sly heroine — played by a brave hen named Feri, in addition to her seven indistinguishable stunt doubles — makes a daring escape when her captor stops his truck to refuel. But she’s snapped up again by the teeth of a dog named Titan, who carries the chicken back to the ramshackle seaside restaurant where his owner (Yannis Kokiasmenos) has much bigger problems than what to serve for dinner.

If the precise contours of those problems are a bit difficult to deduce, that’s probably because — as we’ve already established — this movie is told through the eyes of a chicken. Sometimes literally, thanks to Pálfi’s judicious deployment of POV, which is useful for times when our ruffled protagonist is, say, trapped inside a cardboard box (there’s an excellent bit where the hen starts moving the cardboard box from the inside, a “Metal Gear Solid”-inspired visual gag that proves typical of the director’s wry humor). And what does a chicken know of Europe’s ongoing migrant crisis? Of a protest between angry citizens and riot police? Of human trafficking, and the complications thereof? To judge by the film’s regular assortment of amusingly blank reaction shots, I’d wager “very little.” The titular hen doesn’t even think to look both ways when she crosses the road after flying the coop, let alone have a good answer as to why she’s doing it.

For the most part, the hen is focused on clucking her neck, surviving the pecking order at the restaurant farm where she winds up, and potentially even laying a few eggs of her own someday (we see her hatch in the movie’s first scene, but they grow up so fast). Most of the human drama is relegated to the distant background, as Pálfi mines the humor from his movie’s conceit by using the restaurant as a lens onto the hen’s predicament rather than the other way around. The people are mere archetypes, but some of the animals we meet appear so layered and inscrutable that you’d happily watch a three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about them. (The terse and fiery courtship between the star hen and her most aggressive suitor is soundtracked by a classic Greek love song, a flourish that stands out in a film where desperate migrants are being left for dead just off-camera.)

Then again, couldn’t every film about — and starring — real live animals be considered a documentary to some extent? Feri the chicken has been trained by the best of the business, but she remains blissfully unaware of the camera, and Pálfi takes pains not to anthropomorphize her any more than necessary. Plenty of heightened enjoyment comes elsewhere, much of it laundered through Giorgos Karvelas’ saturated cinematography, Szabolcs Szoke’s hyper-dynamic score, and the furtive way Pálfi bends the film’s crafts into something that almost resembles a chicken’s idea of a Western.

Here, the hen is a hen is a hen, and while “Hen” is prone to long and repetitive stretches in which she basically just hens around as a result of that approach, the animal’s natural obliviousness is too crucial a contrast to our own willful antipathy for Pálfi to risk muddying the difference between the two. At the risk of making the movie’s side-eyed social commentary sound more didactic than it is in practice (save for one very pointed moment towards the end that explicitly affirms Herzog’s claim), “Hen” uses a chicken’s lack of moral responsibility to highlight the mandate we have to heed our own, no matter how effectively we’ve evolved to ignore it.

No matter how good we get at farming other species, and killing our own. Pálfi does very little to goose or otherwise manipulate our emotional attachment to his chicken star, but there’s still something to be said for how easily we become more invested in this witless hen’s fate than in that of the doomed people with whom she crosses paths. By the time it reaches its end, this strange but sober film starts to point back to the beginning, cutting from a single egg being squeezed out of a hen’s vent (Google says “vent”) to a vast sea of them bobbling around inside the factory’s machines. One is easy to follow, and to care about. Thousands are a statistic. We’re smart enough to farm other animals, but people — like chickens — won’t hesitate to eat each other the minute they get hungry.

Dekanalog will release “Hen” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

None of this was ever officially confirmed, however, and in August 2026, we learned that Marvel had cast "Kraven the Hunter" star Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, confirming that Skarsgård wouldn't be making his MCU debut with the X-Men movie. He does, however, quite like the idea of appearing as John Constantine in James Gunn's DC Universe.

The writer/director previously produced, wrote, and directed the 2023 crime thriller "The Last Stop in Yuma County," and is now working on the upcoming "Evil Dead Wrath," a prequel to the bloody good time that was 2026's "Evil Dead Burn." He's received praise from franchise creator Sam Raimi, who described Galluppi as "a storyteller who knows when to keep us waiting in simmering tension and when to hit us with explosive violence."

Created by writer Alan Moore and artists Steve Bissette and John Totleben, John Constantine first appeared in 1985's "The Saga of the Swamp Thing" #37. The British detective and exorcist is known for his incongruous mix of cynicism and deep commitment to helping those in need, and it seems Bill Skarsgård is eager to put his spin on the character.

While Galliuppi works on his script, there's no word from DC Studios on who might star in the film. But Skarsgård's idea of teaming up with his "It" director Andy Muschietti isn't a bad shout. The pair obviously have the horror bonafides, and Skarsgård seems perfect for the role of a conflicted anti-hero with a supernatural element. For now, we'll have to wait to see whether Galluppi's script works out and whether DC Studios also brings him on as director. But studio co-heads James Gunn and Peter Safran would do well to at least consider Skarsgård's vision.

#3576. ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups

There are dozens of scenes that capture “North of North’s” digestible, defiant kindness, but my favorite arrives near the start of the second season’s second episode. Siaja (Anna Lambe) wakes up, grabs a glass of water, and promptly spits it out. The local water supply is contaminated (“They must’ve cranked those chemicals again,” her mom says), so Siaja heads to the nearest store to load up on jugs of clean water. Outside, there’s an elderly woman perched on her snowmobile, smoking a cigarette, who loudly hassles Siaja for a little charity.

“Must be nice,” the woman shouts, getting Siaja’s attention. “[You] buying filtered water. It’s too expensive [for me]. [I] gotta drink government pool water. Back in the day, we had nice ice straight from the river. Pure, nice, and healthy.” Related Stories ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

On that last word, “healthy,” the woman takes a drag from her cigarette, and while she’s doubled over coughing, Siaja takes her forceful hint and puts one of her water jugs in the woman’s cart. “Here, you take this,” Siaja says. The woman, speaking in Inuktitut, does not say “thank you”; she asks if she can keep the jug. Then she hacks a loogie into the snow as Siaja drives off, punctuating just how little the gesture means to her.

Now, it’s clear this woman knows exactly what she’s doing. She didn’t end up outside the town’s only source for clean water by accident, and Siaja knows it. But she also knows the woman is telling the truth: She’s too old to get ice for herself, and she’s too poor to afford purified water. Siaja also knows this woman is her elder, and elders should be taken care of. So after acquiescing in the moment, Siaja expands on the idea soon after: She grabs Alistair (Jay Ryan), her big, burly dad, and they go get blocks of ice from the river to deliver around town — for free.

Of course, it doesn’t go exactly as planned (the rivers aren’t all “pure” and “healthy” anymore), but Siaja’s chance encounter with the woman serves as the impetus for the entire episode: Siaja uses it to prove to her boss that she can be more than an assistant at the community center. She bonds with her dad, who she’s still getting to know. She sets a good example for her daughter, Bun (Keira Belle Cooper), and she still finds time to flirt with her crush, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), in between deliveries.

Siaja is doing exactly what she set out to do from the start of the season: “level up” her life.

Reading it back now, the story sounds corny. But despite all that positive energy driving so many warm-hearted gestures, “North by North” never becomes saccharine. Siaja’s triumphs don’t feel like cheap schmaltz. They hit that tricky TV sweet spot, where characters’ helpful actions and benevolent intentions feel genuine even when, on paper, they seem too nice to be tolerable.

It helps, of course, that Siaja fucks up early and often. Nothing makes a win land like taking many embarrassing losses to get there, as she did in Season 1 after summoning the courage to leave her husband, get a job, and start fresh — with an adorable daughter in tow. In Season 2, her plan to charm tourists doesn’t go over as whimsically as she imagined. Her plan to get her own place doesn’t include dropping in the rankings on an endless waiting list for affordable housing. Her plan to ditch her small-minded ex-husband (who doesn’t appear in Season 2) doesn’t include sitting for rounds of speed-dating or waiting out a relationship that may never end.

Siaja’s self-actualization isn’t as easy as ditching the zero to get with the hero, even when she’s her own hero from the jump — it takes time to learn the ins and outs of public service, to connect with people, and to make sense of your own emotions. “North of North” respects each process while savoring her struggle through them. (Lambe’s comic timing remains pitch-perfect, and her ability to navigate tonal swings is just as sharp.)

Investing in Siaja’s incremental progress does wonders to keep “North of North” from feeling like forgettable fluff — especially when the back-half of Season 2 gets heavy wrestling with familial, cultural, and communal responsibilities — but none of it work without the attention to detail surrounding Siaja, too. When the first season premiered in January 2025, “North by North” earned plenty of well-deserved praise for its authenticity. The fictional town of Ice Cove represents real communities in Nunavet, the northernmost part of Canada within the Arctic Circle, and the series employed a heavily Indigenous cast and crew to help bring it to life.

And what life there is: Season 2 is rich with cultural specifics, from a Greenlandic mask-dancing celebration to public safety concerns. (Beyond the bad water, don’t forget to place your beer orders early! A birthday without a brewski could be your last!) Every episode whisks you away to a very cold, very kind small town, which is oh-so-welcoming on chilly winter evenings when you just want to bask in the season’s cozy glow.

Respecting and highlighting Inuk customs is step one. Step two expands the idea by grounding “North by North” in perspectives beyond their beloved lead screwup. That way, her work ethic and generosity stay sweet and meaningful (when overexposure could easily turn them sour) and the show’s overall tone avoids becoming rote. Siaja’s mom, Neevee (Maika Harper), is the sardonic balance her daughter demands, and how they flesh out her backstory to explain her sharp disposition offers some of the season’s strongest scenes. Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), Siaja’s boss, is an oblivious white lady desperate to be cherished as a leader, and her pushy ambitions help clarify Siaja’s unselfish aid to others (while generating laughs).

And then there’s the townsfolk, who may not always be as colorful as the woman demanding free water, but who share her fair yet formidable spirit. If Siaja’s community service was met with cheers and applause, it would be unbelievable. That’s not how citizens treat their local officials. But their measured disposition isn’t just authentic, it’s essential. Similarly, if the citizens were the butt of every joke (like in “Parks and Recreation”), Siaja’s dedication could feel misplaced. If they were mean, like too many real-life city council visitors, her above-and-beyond gestures could seem foolish. Instead, Siaja’s community is just there, living their own lives, waiting for her to get her shit together and do what’s right by them.

“North of North” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

#3574. Avengers: Doomsday's Final Writing Credits Confirmed, With Two Marvel Actors Reportedly Involved

With so many moving parts in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, it's perhaps inevitable that the movie scripts are always changing, too. That's especially true for the incoming team-up movie "Avengers: Doomsday," which features a dizzying array of superheroes alongside the return of Robert Downey Jr., not as Iron Man but as classic Marvel villain Doctor Doom. Directors Anthony and Joe Russo have confirmed the reports that the "Doomsday" script was still being written while they were filming, describing themselves as "improvisation-based, rehearsal-based directors."

Even after filming is complete, it takes a while to determine which writers meet the criteria for a writing credit, per the Writers Guild of America's credit system. The WGA recently confirmed the two writers who will be given the main "written by" credit for "Avengers: Doomsday." One is Stephen McFeely, an MCU mainstay who co-wrote "Captain America: The First Avenger," "Avengers: Infinity War" and "Endgame," and several other titles. The other is Michael Waldron, who wrote the script for "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness" and created the well-received Disney+ series "Loki."

With a movie production as big as "Doomsday," however, there's almost always a hidden team of writers and script doctors who are brought in to help fine-tune and troubleshoot the script, or who worked on previous versions of it. And with an improvisational approach to production, actors will often add their own contributions via ad-libbing. Now, rumor has it that two actors in "Avengers: Doomsday" contributed enough to get an extra credit.

X/Twitter user Crystal4KQual, who has proven to be a reliable source for Marvel scoops, shared this tidbit: "I recently learned through their production companies, Ryan [Reynolds] and Hugh [Jackman] may get some form of screen writing credits on '[Avengers:] Doomsday,' too."

This wouldn't be the first writing credit for Reynolds, who co-wrote "Deadpool 2" and "Deadpool & Wolverine" alongside Rhett Reese and Paul Wernick. Actors aren't typically given writing credits just for ad-libbing some of their lines (or Reynolds would have a lot more credits to his name). However, in 2022, the Writers Guild of America introduced a new "additional literary material" credit for people who provided writing services for a movie but would otherwise be uncredited. The credit doesn't come with any residuals and doesn't equate to authorship (a writer can get an ALM credit even if none of their contributions end up on screen), but it does allow writers to put the experience on their resume.

"The Fantastic Four: First Steps," for example, had seven writers credited for additional literary material, including "Doomsday" screenwriter Michael Waldron. Indeed, given its complex development history, "Avengers: Doomsday" may end up with a similar number of ALM credits, including the "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" writing team of Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers, who were reported to have worked on the script.

We'll find out if Reynolds and Jackman did manage to snag any writing credits when "Avengers: Doomsday" hits theaters on December 18, 2026.

Even Halo Infinite isn't quite ready to call it quits, continuing to receive unexpected updates this year despite its major content support coming to an end.

Now, fans looking for even more Halo content have another release to look forward to this holiday season. A new book collection bringing together three classic novels from the franchise is on the way, giving longtime fans and newcomers a chance to revisit some of Master Chief's most important adventures.

Titled Halo: The Master Chief Omnibus, the hardcover collection arrives on Nov. 10, from Gallery Books. It brings together three bestselling novels by authors Eric Nylund and William C. Dietz, alongside a new foreword and additional material.

The new omnibus collects three novels that helped establish the Halo universe's expanded lore: The Fall of Reach and First Strike by Eric Nylund, and The Flood by William C. Dietz.

Originally published as stand-alone books, the novels explore different stages of humanity's war against the Covenant, the alien religious empire threatening humanity's survival. They also provide additional context for Master Chief, the Spartan super-soldier better known as John-117, and the events surrounding the original Halo trilogy.

The collection offers a broad look at the early days of the Halo storyline, starting with the origins of the Spartan program and eventually moving into the conflict that puts humanity's survival at stake.

The Fall of Reach explores the creation and training of the Spartan-II program, including John-117's transformation into the Master Chief. It also chronicles the Covenant's devastating attack on the human military stronghold of Reach, an important event in the franchise's history.

The Flood retells the events of the original Halo: Combat Evolved, expanding on the Master Chief's fight against the Covenant on the mysterious Halo ringworld. The story also introduces the terrifying Flood, a parasitic lifeform that poses an even greater threat to the galaxy.

Finally, First Strike bridges the events of Halo: Combat Evolved and Halo 2. Following the destruction of the first Halo ring, Master Chief and other survivors attempt to return to Earth while uncovering more about the Covenant's plans.

Together, the three novels provide a deeper understanding of the characters, conflicts, and major events that shaped the original Halo games. Halo: The Master Chief Omnibus releases in hardcover on Nov. 10.

Keanu Reeves played Constantine in the eponymous 2005 "Constantine" film. Reeves himself has been pushing for a "Constantine" sequel, but "Constantine 2" has kept facing delays. With DC Studios moving forward with a new Constantine, it's unclear if Reeves' sequel will continue; Deadline's reporting does not mention the project one way or another. Co-created in 1985 by Alan Moore, Stephen R. Bissette, and John Totleben, John Constantine first debuted as a supporting character in "Swamp Thing." Just a few years later, he earned a spin-off comic, "Hellblazer," that ran for 25 years and 300 issues.

As for Constantine, he's a warlock, an occult detective, an exorcist, and a con man known for his acerbic cynicism and chain-smoking. (Noted "Hellblazer" arc "Dangerous Habits" by Garth Ennis and Will Simpson is all about John discovering he has lung cancer from his constant smoking and racing to save himself.) While initially presented as part of the main DC Universe, "Hellblazer," published by DC's Vertigo imprint, gradually drifted into its own separate world.

But then, DC Comics' 2011 reboot "The New 52" broke down those walls again. Suddenly, John was joining the Justice League Dark, a team for DC's supernatural superheroes. That integration carried over outside the comics. Welsh actor Matt Ryan played Constantine in a short-lived NBC series in 2014 — but that was only the beginning. Ryan guest-starred as John in Season 4 of "Arrow" and then became a regular on "Legends of Tomorrow." He also became the character's official voice actor in animation, beginning with a 2017 "Justice League Dark" animated movie.

This early, it's unclear who DC Studios could have in mind to play John Constantine, though actor Bill Skarsgård has put himself in contention. It's worth noting that DC Studios currently has a "Swamp Thing" movie, directed by James Mangold, in the works. This is pure speculation, but it wouldn't be out of place for John to show up in that.

#3570. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973.  Related Stories ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies.

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre.

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker.

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters.

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down.

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket.

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy.

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him.

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter.

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3568. Godzilla Minus Zero Has Two Cameos Only Hardcore Franchise Fans Noticed

The following post contains brief spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is pure Godzilla spectacle. This is a bigger, badder king of the monsters that's not without its flaws, but nevertheless offers enough spectacle and kaiju action to make it a thrilling cinematic experience. Sure, we've had plenty of kaiju movies the past decade, but few manage to get anywhere near the scope or scale that Takashi Yamazaki offers in his follow-up to the Oscar-winning "Godzilla Minus One."

One of the things that makes this movie special is how it expands the world of the previous Godzilla. By bringing in King Ghidorah (whose design unfortunately leaked online before the film's release), the movie throws open the doors to all sorts of Toho kaiju. It's significant that it's Ghidorah who becomes Godzilla's first foe here, because the three-headed alien dragon that shoots gravity-affecting lightning is such a weird creature that it allows for pretty much anything to follow him. From here, you could easily do Mechagodzilla, or Mothra, or even Gigan.

That being said, "Godzilla Minus Zero" remains a surprisingly grounded and human movie even if it deals with extraterrestrial threats. This is a film with some of the most harrowing kaiju imagery in decades, as it shows how truly horrific the aftermath of a Godzilla attack would actually be. It's unlike any Godzilla movie we've had in this new era. This feels like classic Godzilla without trying to reinvent the wheel, and it feels more grounded than the bonkers and silly MonsterVerse.

Which is why it's funny that this movie features two cameos from two very different corners of the Godzilla franchise — cameos only hardcore fans will notice. Specifically, the film features cameos from directors Hideaki Anno and Jordan Vogt-Roberts.

Hideaki Anno is a legend of anime, having created the groundbreaking and hugely influential "Neon Genesis Evangelion." But Anno is above all else a massive nerd who's spent the past decade bringing every one of his childhood obsessions to life on the big screen, starting with "Shin Godzilla," and then with "Shin Ultraman" and "Shin Kamen Rider." Anno's "Shin Godzilla" was a revelation, a political satire about the failures of government to respond to a crisis that also happened to feature a terrifying Godzilla.

Anno has a blink-and-you-miss-it cameo in "Godzilla Minus Zero" when Koichi and Noriko leave Tokyo and are on a train south. The camera lingers for less than a second on a man reading a newspaper containing news of Ghidorah's attack. That man is the legend behind "Shin Godzilla."

Jordan Vogt-Roberts' cameo comes at the very end of the film when a group of American soldiers capture professor Murakami. What makes his cameo interesting is that Vogt-Roberts has not actually directed a Godzilla project. Instead, he's best known for directing "Kong: Skull Island," which is a very fun take on a kaiju movie and is part of the MonsterVerse, but doesn't actually feature the King of the Monsters himself.

Speaking with The Hollywood Reporter, director "Godzilla Minus Zero" director Takashi Yamazaki explained how Vogt-Roberts ended up in the final film.

"Jordan makes quite frequent trips to Japan. During one of his trips, he reached out to us, and we set up a dinner," Yamazaki said. "That's when he said, 'Hey, I'd really love to be in the next Godzilla movie you're working on.' And I said, 'Well, if you're in Japan, perhaps there's a scene we could work you into.'"

#3566. 49 Years Later, Steven Spielberg’s Sci-Fi Thriller Masterpiece Is Officially Free on YouTube

Make a big batch of mashed potatoes and sit down to watch

Most creators are lucky if they ever make one truly revolutionary thing in their lives. Steven Spielberg has made at least six.

He's had his misfires and genuine failures along the way, but Spielberg has reshaped multiple genres and filmmaking as a whole in his wake. Many of his movies have become part of the bedrock of worldwide culture. There are multiple different trends and revivals that can be traced straight back to Spielberg, from Indiana Jones' faux-serial period action to Saving Private Ryan redefining war films to virtually every monster movie made after 1975.

In retrospect, however, there's one entertainment subgenre that we might not give Spielberg enough credit for, and that's the alien conspiracy thriller. 1977's Close Encounters of the Third Kind was Spielberg's second big hit after Jaws. While it hasn't latched onto the popular imagination in quite the way that some of Spielberg's later films did, it's hard not to see Close Encounters' influence on the subsequent alien-abduction films and TV of the 1980s and 1990s.

If you're interested in seeing Close Encounters for yourself in advance of its 50th anniversary, YouTube is currently airing it for free, albeit with ads. Even better, YouTube's version is the Spielberg-endorsed Director's Cut from 1998, which reverses some changes that were made to the film in its 1980 Special Edition.

When I was a kid, I always thought Close Encounters was the third film in a series, based solely upon the title. In fact, the name comes from the 1972 book The UFO Experience: A Scientific Inquiry, by J. Allen Hynek. Hynek was a scientific consultant on Close Encounters, and even makes a cameo at one point in the film. (Look for the guy at Devils Tower smoking the pipe.)

In his book, Hynek proposed a scale of classification for UFO sightings, which ranged from #1 (strange lights in the sky) to #6 (encountering a UFO that comes alongside an 'animated entity,' such as a human pilot or genuine alien). The latter three stages on Hynek's scale are labeled as "close encounters," the last and most significant of which, the “third kind,” provided the final name for the film. It’s another term for what’s now more commonly called “first contact.”

Close Encounters opens in 1977, as multiple lost aircraft have suddenly reappeared in the middle of the California desert. As a team of scientists tries to figure out what's happened, multiple UFOs are sighted all over the world.

In Muncie, Indiana, Roy Neary (Richard Dreyfuss) is called out to address a local power outage. While working, a near-miss from a passing UFO burns half of Roy's face.

After that encounter, Roy quickly becomes obsessed with the UFOs, which endangers his relationship with his wife Ronnie (Teri Garr) and their children. Without any idea why, Roy is increasingly compelled to make models and sculptures of a specific mountain with whatever's handy, from dirt to clay to mashed potatoes. What Roy doesn't know is that his new hobby is about to intersect with what's become a genuine conspiracy.

There are parts of Close Encounters that can be a genuinely rough sit. While the audience knows that Roy is on to something, due to how his obsessions intersect with other characters and scenes, Roy himself doesn't. The second act of the movie is a portrait of psychological disintegration, as Roy himself doesn't know what's happened to him. He ends up alone in his house at one point, surrounded by news clippings and handmade models, in a scene that presages all the great conspiracy-board scenes in later pop culture, from The X-Files to that famous meme of Charlie Day from It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia. In retrospect, Roy Neary is a prototype for what’s since become a famous stock character in Western fiction: the conspiracy-monger who’s just looking for that one last “I told you so!” that will prove them right.

That might be why Close Encounters has faded slightly in the popular imagination. It's a science fiction movie, but it doesn't have the spectacle or excitement of Spielberg's later work in the genre. In fact, he revisited the topic of alien conspiracies himself five years later with E.T., which, in retrospect, might've overshadowed what hype Close Encounters may have had. Richard Dreyfuss going slowly insane at the family dinner table isn't quite as iconic an image as E.T.'s bicycle chase.

Just the same, Close Encounters is a classic for a reason, and almost 50 years later, you can make a real case that the real conspiracy is how a movie this good ever wound up becoming so overlooked. As long as you know going in that it's closer to a strange family drama than any kind of thriller, it's worth seeing Close Encounters of the Third Kind at least once. It's an underrated linchpin of the last 50 years in science fiction.

Close Encounters of the Third Kind’s Director's Cut is currently streaming on YouTube.

#3565. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3564. Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained: Where The Franchise Goes From Here

Full spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero" follow.

For the longest time in the character's 72-year history, the "Godzilla" films were surprisingly light on continuity. During the Showa era films produced by Toho Studios during the 1950s through the 1970s, the most common recurring characters in the movies were the kaiju themselves. When the Heisei era occurred between 1984 and 1996, they established a continuity that was a bit more contiguous, but not much. The Millennium era became even more piecemeal continuity-wise, with most entries using the original 1954 "Godzilla" as a starting point but erasing everything else until the latest film (similar to how the "Halloween" franchise continuity has operated before). Even the MonsterVerse films produced by Legendary Pictures function most similarly to the Heisei era in terms of continuity, while Toho's 2016 "Shin Godzilla" is basically a one-shot.

All of this is to say that the "Godzilla" franchise is wildly unpredictable where canon is concerned, with each film or groups of films essentially treating it piecemeal. It's exceedingly rare that a true sequel has been made to a "Godzilla" film in the past, where a prior movie's cast and filmmakers have returned for a second round. That milestone has finally been achieved with "Godzilla Minus Zero."

The movie is an unabashed sequel to 2023's "Godzilla Minus One," as it's once again written and directed by Takashi Yamazaki. As such, it's a beautifully rich experience previously unseen in most "Godzilla" movies, one which builds from its predecessor in a big way. "Minus Zero" isn't just another "Godzilla" adventure, but a movie which continues the "Minus" series' character arcs and themes, and its emotional, somewhat cliffhanger-style conclusion indicates that the story may not be over yet.

"Godzilla Minus One" takes place between 1945 and 1947, during the immediate aftermath of World War II. Japan's loss of the war has left it hurting in more ways than one, with the country having to muddle through dire straits both physical and emotional. This is represented by the ensemble of characters we meet, chief among them Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a kamikaze pilot who deserts his suicidal duty, Noriko Ōishi (Minami Hamabe), a woman who takes it upon herself to rescue and raise an orphan girl, Akiko (Sae Nagatani), and Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), a Naval weapons engineer.

All three adults come to view the superpowered creature Godzilla as emblematic of their personal struggles. For Noda, Godzilla must be stopped for Japan to have a future. For Noriko, Godzilla is something to be survived. For Shikishima, Godzilla is the personification of his guilt, as well as a force of death and destruction who must be vanquished.

After Noriko's apparent demise during a Godzilla attack on Ginza, Noda spearheads a civilian-run mission in which a couple of Navy destroyers will alternately sink and raise Godzilla at dangerous speeds. As a failsafe, Shikishima has volunteered to fly one of the last available Shinden fighters to lure Godzilla out to sea. However, his real plan is to fly the plane, loaded with explosives, directly into Godzilla's mouth. He does so, but uses an ejection seat to escape at the last minute, proving he's overcome his guilt and has decided to live. Following the Godzilla victory, Shikishima learns that Noriko has in fact survived, and he and Akiko go to visit her in the hospital. As Noriko tearfully reunites with her new family, a mysterious black mark on her neck shimmers.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" picks up in 1949, when Noda is informed of another giant monster attacking Japan: Ghidorah. As Noda and his new advisor, meterologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), plan to kill Ghidorah with lightning, Noda asks Shikishima for help. Shikishima tries to stay out of the battle for the sake of his now-wife Noriko and adopted daughter Akiko, especially as he and Noriko are the only ones who know that she survived Ginza due to being infected with Godzilla's cells, which might lead to her death soon.

Yet when Ghidorah survives the initial attack and a now-regenerated Godzilla reappears, Noda and biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), a survivor of the Hiroshima bombing, decide the best plan is to lure Godzilla and Ghidorah into a deathmatch fight, with the humans killing the victor. To do this, Murakami has a device which means only Noriko and her G cells can "call" Godzilla.

Shikishima and Noriko agree to the plan, unaware that Murakami intends to later use Noriko as a way to get revenge on the USA. Godzilla and Ghidorah fight in Ginza, and the former eventually triumphs, though at the expense of Noda's life. When the Japanese army gives orders that Godzilla is not to be killed, Shikishima and Noriko mutiny against Murakami. However, Murakami reveals that Noda recently convinced him of the error of his ways, and the couple are allowed to escape while the scientist destroys his machine and his work.

Unfortunately, Murakami's good deed is punished when the US army arrests him. Meanwhile, Shikishima and Noriko try to abandon Akiko, knowing they're doomed to a life on the run from the authorities. Yet they ultimately can't leave her behind, and ride off as a family to an uncertain future.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is a true second chapter in a continuing story. This is a fairly unprecedented occurrence in the Godzilla franchise, not just in the way the returning characters are built upon and expanded, but also in the way Takashi Yamazaki continues the themes from "Minus One." Rather than jumping ahead in time too far, "Minus Zero" is still a story of post-war Japan, and nowhere is this more evident than in Kanji Murakami's character.

Although Godzilla is shifted toward a more heroic light, as has happened many times over the franchise, he's still presented as morally dubious. If, in "Minus One," Godzilla stood for the sins of the Japanese (if not all humanity) come to punish them, "Minus Zero" looks at Godzilla as the country's answer to the atomic bomb: a destructive and ultimately uncontrollable weapon which should only be used as a last resort, if ever.

In addition to the war allegory, "Godzilla Minus Zero" takes the characters of "Minus One" beyond their absolution in that film. Much of "Minus Zero" concerns whether the happy (or relatively happy) future the survivors of that movie fought so hard for can even happen, as everything from the Ghidorah attacks to the potentially deadly G Cells in Noriko's body appears like an insurmountable threat. Yet while unfortunate consequences are unavoidable, Yamazaki's optimism ultimately shines through, especially in the way the bonds between the characters mean that all hope is never lost. Even the supporting cast from "Minus One," though given smaller roles here, contribute to this theme. The implication is that Japan, if not humanity, can have a bright future if everyone supports each other and serves their better natures rather than being selfish or hateful.

If "Godzilla Minus Zero" were to conclude the "Minus" continuity, then both "Godzilla Minus One" and "Minus Zero" would serve as a fully satisfying tale. Still, Takashi Yamazaki does leave "Minus Zero" on several cliffhangers, or at least unresolved questions. The ending leaves the ultimate fate of many characters uncertain, chief among them Murakami and the Shikishima family. In the case of the former, it seems likely that the US army intend to make Murakami work for them to get Godzilla under American control.

In the case of the latter, the Shikishimas are now going to be on the run, and it's unclear what their plan is to evade the government(s). It's neat how these films have set up so much good material with the human characters that there's enough interest in what happens to them before one even considers the kaiju.

But oh, the giant monsters! We cannot forget about them. Now that Yamazaki has introduced Ghidorah, the door is open for any other Toho-verse kaiju to turn up. In terms of the themes that the "Minus" films are dealing with, it would feel appropriate for other heavily allegorical beasts like Rodan or Hedorah to make their appearance. Although the MonsterVerse's "Godzilla vs. Kong" recently used Mechagodzilla as humanity's warmongering response to Godzilla, such a characterization would fit snugly into the "Minus" films, too. And, while "Minus Zero" only contains a fantasy sequence of Godzilla attacking NYC, there's the chance that the action could expand beyond Japan for real. While it's not clear whether there will be another "Minus" film at all yet, there's certainly no dearth of possibilities for one to explore.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3563. ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites. Related Stories ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

#3562. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.
